A pragmatic guide to zero-downtime cloud migration

CloudBy the OneClicq team9 November 20267 min read

For a system your business runs on every day, the hardest part of a cloud migration is not the cloud. It is moving without customers, staff or partners noticing. That is a planning problem, and it can be solved.

1. Know exactly what you are moving

Start with an inventory of every application, database, scheduled job, file share and integration. For each one, write down who owns it, what depends on it, how much downtime the business can tolerate, and how much data changes per hour. Hidden dependencies, such as a nightly export another team relies on, cause more failed migrations than any technical issue.

2. Choose a migration pattern per system

  • Rehost ("lift and shift"): move virtual machines largely as they are. Fastest, least change, fewest cloud savings.
  • Replatform: keep the application but move to managed services, such as a managed database or app hosting. A good balance for most business systems.
  • Refactor: rebuild parts of the application for the cloud. Highest benefit and highest effort; best saved for systems with a clear business case.
  • Retire or replace: some systems are better switched off or replaced by a SaaS product.

Mixing patterns is normal. Rehost the low-risk systems first to build confidence, and refactor only where it pays.

3. Build the landing zone first

Before moving any workload, set up the foundations in AWS or Azure: accounts or subscriptions, networking, identity and access, backups, logging, monitoring and cost alerts. Doing this once, properly, prevents every later migration from inventing its own security rules.

4. Keep data in sync until cut-over

Downtime usually comes from the database. Instead of a long "stop, copy, start" window, replicate data continuously from the old system to the new one, using the database's own replication or a managed migration service. When it is time to switch, only the last few seconds of changes need to catch up.

5. Run both environments side by side

With data in sync, test the new environment with real traffic before anyone depends on it. Common approaches are:

  • Read-only shadowing: send copies of real requests to the new system and compare results.
  • Gradual traffic shifting: move a small share of users first, using DNS weighting or a load balancer, then increase.
  • Blue-green switch: keep the old ("blue") environment running and switch everyone to the new ("green") one at once, with a one-step switch back.

6. Plan the cut-over like a launch

  1. Lower DNS time-to-live values a few days before, so changes take effect quickly.
  2. Freeze non-essential changes to both environments.
  3. Write a step-by-step runbook with owners, timings and checks for each step.
  4. Choose a low-traffic window and tell support teams in advance.
  5. Agree a clear rollback trigger, such as error rates above an agreed level, and rehearse the rollback.

7. Don't switch off the old system too early

Keep the old environment available, read-only, for an agreed period after cut-over. Check reports, month-end processes and integrations that only run occasionally before you decommission anything.

8. Tune costs after you land

Cloud bills often rise straight after migration because servers are sized for the old peak. Once you have a few weeks of real usage data, right-size instances, schedule non-production environments to switch off at night, and commit to reserved capacity only for steady workloads.

The takeaway

Zero-downtime migration comes from preparation: a complete inventory, continuous data sync, testing with real traffic and a rehearsed rollback. With those in place, cut-over night becomes routine rather than risky.
